data.title: Disconnected Remote Desktop Sessions Can Be Hijacked
data.summary:
Disconnected Remote Desktop sessions belonging to other users, including administrators,
could be resumed from a compromised host without any credential.
data.description:
A disconnected session is still a live logon. An account with SYSTEM on the host can attach
to it and inherit the user's identity without knowing or capturing a password, which makes
this one of the few escalation routes that defeats credential controls completely.

The impact depends on who left a session behind. Where administrators connect to servers
and disconnect rather than signing out, their sessions remain available to anyone who later
compromises that host, which inverts the usual direction of trust.

Session timeout policy is the control, and it is routinely set generously or not at all
because signing out is inconvenient.
data.recommendation:
* Configure disconnected session limits so sessions are signed out rather than left
  indefinitely.
* Require administrators to sign out rather than disconnect, and enforce it through policy.
* Alert on session connect events where the connecting account differs from the session
  owner.
* Avoid administrative logons to hosts of lower trust, which is what makes the session
  available in the first place.
data.short_recommendation: Enforce disconnected session timeouts and alert on cross-account session connects.
